title: Hand hygiene
blurb: The three levels of hand hygiene, the WHO 5 moments, the handwash technique step by step, and why you work bare below the elbows.
question: You finish assisting with a filling, peel off your gloves and reach for the computer keyboard to update the appointment. Your colleague, who is wearing a watch and gel nails, says gloves kept your hands clean anyway. What should you do, and what would you say to her?

teach.h: Hands are the main route of cross-infection
teach.body: Your hands touch patients, instruments, the chair, the light, the keyboard and the phone, so they are the commonest way micro-organisms move from one place to another. Skin carries two groups of micro-organisms. Transient micro-organisms are picked up from what you touch; they sit on the surface and are easily passed on, but also easily removed. Resident micro-organisms live in the deeper layers of the skin and are harder to remove. Good hand hygiene removes the transients every time.

rows.label: When
values: Start and end of session, visibly dirty hands, after the toilet
Before and after each patient, around glove use

teach.h: The WHO 5 moments for hand hygiene
teach.caption: Moments 1 and 2 protect the patient. Moments 3, 4 and 5 protect you and the environment.

teach.body: Clean your hands before you put on gloves and start treatment, and again straight after you take gloves off. Gloves can have tiny holes, and your hands get contaminated as you remove them, so gloves never replace hand hygiene. Clean your hands immediately after glove removal and before you touch the phone, keyboard or patient notes. And clean them after touching the chair, light or bracket table, even if you didn't touch the patient.

steps.label: Wet hands, then apply soap
steps.sub: Enough to cover all hand surfaces

steps.label: Backs of hands
steps.sub: Palm over back, fingers interlaced; swap

steps.label: Between and behind fingers
steps.sub: Fingers interlaced; backs of fingers into palms

steps.label: Thumbs and fingertips
steps.sub: Rotational rubbing in the opposite palm

steps.label: Rinse and dry
steps.sub: Single-use paper towel; turn the tap off with it

teach.caption: Alcohol hand rub uses the same rubbing steps on dry hands, until the rub has dried.

items.label: handwash with soap and water, start to finish
alcohol hand rub, until hands are dry

teach.h: Bare below the elbows: ready for clinic?

rows.label: Cut covered with a waterproof dressing

teach.note: Jewellery and artificial nails trap micro-organisms, stop you cleaning properly and can puncture gloves. Some practice policies allow a plain band ring.

teach.body: Frequent washing and glove use can leave hands dry and cracked, and broken skin is both a portal of entry and a home for micro-organisms. Wet your hands before applying soap, rinse well, pat them completely dry and use the practice's emollient hand cream. If your skin becomes sore, red or cracked, report it so occupational health can assess you.

teach.text: Alcohol hand rub is not suitable for visibly dirty or blood-stained hands; wash with soap and water instead. And gloves are never a substitute for hand hygiene: clean your hands before putting them on and after taking them off.

items: Social, antiseptic and surgical hand hygiene remove progressively more micro-organisms.
WHO 5 moments: before patient, before clean procedure, after body fluid risk, after patient, after surroundings.
Clean hands immediately after removing gloves, before touching phones, keyboards or notes.
Handwash 40–60 seconds; alcohol rub 20–30 seconds; turn taps off with the paper towel.
Bare below the elbows: no watches, jewelled rings or artificial nails.

summary: You can now choose between social, antiseptic and surgical hand hygiene, apply the WHO 5 moments to chairside work, carry out the handwash technique in the right order and time, and explain why watches, jewellery and artificial nails have no place in clinic.

A.q: After removing her gloves at the end of treatment, a nurse immediately answers the surgery phone. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Her hands will be dried out
Nothing, gloves kept her hands clean
Only her own skin is at risk
A.why: Hands are contaminated during glove removal, so touching the phone transfers micro-organisms to a surface others use.

whyNot.0: Dry skin isn't the immediate concern; contamination of the phone is.
whyNot.1: Gloves can have tiny holes and hands are contaminated as gloves come off.
whyNot.2: The phone becomes contaminated and puts everyone who uses it at risk.

A.q: Which level of hand hygiene is used before a surgical procedure such as placing an implant?
A.why: Surgical hand antisepsis covers the hands and forearms and reduces resident as well as transient micro-organisms.

whyNot.0: A social handwash removes dirt and transients but is not enough for surgery.
whyNot.2: A standard alcohol rub is antiseptic-level, not a surgical scrub.
whyNot.3: An antiseptic handwash is used between routine patients, not before surgery.

A.q: A team member wears long acrylic nails under her gloves. Why is this unsuitable?
options: They make gloves hard to choose
They only breach the practice uniform code
They hold germs and can tear gloves
A.why: Artificial nails harbour micro-organisms, stop hands being cleaned properly and increase the risk of glove puncture.

whyNot.0: Choosing gloves is not the issue; infection risk is.
whyNot.1: It is an infection control issue, not just a uniform rule.
whyNot.3: Patient reaction is not the reason; contamination and glove damage are.

B.q: Your glove tears and your hand is visibly stained with blood. Which hand hygiene is appropriate?
options: Wash with liquid soap and water
Rub in alcohol gel until fully dry
Wipe hands with a surface wipe
Put a fresh pair of gloves on
B.why: Visibly soiled hands need washing with soap and water; alcohol rub doesn't work properly on dirty hands.

whyNot.1: Alcohol rub is not suitable for visibly dirty or blood-stained hands.
whyNot.2: Surface wipes are for surfaces and may irritate skin; they are not hand hygiene.
whyNot.3: New gloves over contaminated hands trap the contamination; clean your hands first.

B.q: You have just wiped down the dental chair and light after the patient left. Which of the WHO 5 moments applies?
B.why: Touching the chair, light and other items around the patient is moment 5: after touching patient surroundings.

whyNot.0: The patient has left; you are not about to touch them.
whyNot.1: You are not about to perform a clean or aseptic task.
whyNot.3: This is cleaning the surroundings rather than direct exposure to body fluids.

B.q: A nurse arrives for clinic wearing a jewelled ring and a wristwatch. Why should these be removed?
options: They could be lost in the sink
They stop hands being cleaned well
B.why: Jewellery and watches trap micro-organisms and stop the hands and wrists being cleaned properly.

whyNot.0: Losing them is a nuisance, but the reason is infection control.
whyNot.2: Scratching is possible, but the main reason is effective hand hygiene.
whyNot.3: Glare is not the reason for being bare below the elbows.

C.q: How long should a handwash with soap and water take, from wetting your hands to drying them?
C.why: The WHO technique takes 40–60 seconds in total for a soap and water handwash.

whyNot.0: 5–10 seconds is far too short to cover every surface.
whyNot.1: HTM 01-05 mentions about 15 seconds of rubbing, but the whole handwash, from wetting to drying, takes 40–60 seconds.
whyNot.3: 3–5 minutes is closer to a surgical scrub than a routine handwash.

C.q: After washing your hands at a hand-operated tap, how should you turn it off?
options: Leave it running for the next person
With the cuff of your tunic
With the paper towel you used
C.why: The tap handle was touched with dirty hands, so using the paper towel stops your clean hands being recontaminated.

whyNot.0: Touching the tap handle recontaminates your clean hands.
whyNot.1: Leaving the tap running wastes water and leaves the handle contaminated.
whyNot.2: Your tunic cuff would become contaminated, and you should be bare below the elbows.

C.q: Which statement about alcohol hand rub is correct?
options: It is not suitable on visibly dirty hands
It replaces handwashing in every situation
It can be used on gloves between patients
It must be rinsed off with water afterwards
C.why: Alcohol rub works on clean-looking hands; dirt and blood stop it working, so soiled hands must be washed.

whyNot.1: Soap and water is still needed for visibly dirty hands and at certain times.
whyNot.2: Gloves are single-use and changed between patients, never cleaned with rub.
whyNot.3: Alcohol rub is rubbed in until dry; it isn't rinsed off.

reteach.title: Germs behave like glitter
reteach.question: If you get glitter on your hands, it ends up on everything you touch until you wash it off properly. How does that help you think about hand hygiene?

blocks.body: Imagine every patient's saliva was full of invisible glitter. After treatment it would be on your gloves, and some would get onto your hands as you took the gloves off. Touch the keyboard and the glitter is now there for the next person. A quick rinse wouldn't shift it all: you'd need soap, every surface of your hands, and time. That's why technique, timing and the moments you choose all matter.

blocks.h: Which hand hygiene do I need?

blocks.text: Glove removal is a hand hygiene moment, every time. Clean hands first, then the keyboard.

explain.body: Social handwashing with liquid soap removes dirt and most transient micro-organisms. Antiseptic hand hygiene uses an antimicrobial soap or alcohol rub. Surgical hand antisepsis covers hands and forearms and also reduces resident micro-organisms.

test.q: Which level of hand hygiene uses plain liquid soap and mainly removes dirt and transient micro-organisms?
test.why: A social handwash with liquid soap and water removes dirt and most transient micro-organisms.

whyNot.0: A surgical scrub uses an antimicrobial product and also reduces residents.
whyNot.2: An antiseptic handwash uses an antimicrobial soap, not plain soap.
whyNot.3: Alcohol rub doesn't use soap or water.

explain.body: Before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings.

test.q: You have just removed your gloves after treating a patient. Which moment best applies?
test.why: You have just finished patient contact, so this is moment 4: after touching a patient.

whyNot.0: You've finished with this patient rather than about to start.
whyNot.1: You're not about to do a clean or aseptic task.
whyNot.2: Moment 5 covers the chair and equipment when you haven't touched the patient.

explain.body: Wet hands, apply soap, then rub palms, backs of hands, between fingers, backs of fingers, thumbs and fingertips. Rinse, dry with a single-use paper towel and use it to turn off the tap.

test.q: What is the final step of a correct handwash at a hand-operated tap?
options: Turn the tap off with the paper towel
Shake your hands dry over the sink
Turn the tap off with a clean hand
Dry your hands on your uniform
test.why: Using the paper towel to turn off the tap stops your clean hands touching the dirty tap handle.

whyNot.1: Wet hands spread micro-organisms more easily; dry them with a paper towel.
whyNot.2: The tap handle is contaminated and would undo the handwash.
whyNot.3: Uniforms are not clean drying surfaces.

explain.body: Short sleeves, short natural nails, no watch, no bracelets, no jewelled rings and no artificial nails or varnish. Cover cuts with a waterproof dressing.

test.q: Which of these is acceptable for a dental nurse during a clinical session?
test.why: Short, clean, natural nails allow effective hand hygiene and don't damage gloves.

whyNot.0: Nail varnish can chip and harbour micro-organisms.
whyNot.1: Watches trap micro-organisms and prevent wrists being washed.
whyNot.3: Artificial nails harbour micro-organisms and puncture gloves.
